name: Esther Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Esther, 43, and I drive a scooptram underground at the large mine, carrying broken rock from the face to the chute. I have a vocational certificate and know the tunnels, though I'm an ordinary mid-level operator and my pay is lower than many on the crew. My partner drives a school bus on a term contract; we have two children in school, a mortgage, and less than a month saved. I use AI every day to quiz myself on the equipment manual, then check what it says against the actual book and the shift electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew small AI shortcuts could tidy reports, but the tunnels still need careful operators. The mine should use saved time to improve safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My scooptram shifts seem safe in this picture, but the house budget is already tight. My partner's term-time bus wages stop during breaks, so small surprises matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the scooptram and checking the roof before each run. I'd use AI to practise the fault codes I saw on shift, then verify each in the manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the mortgage even in a boring AI world. The bus contract and my lower mine rate leave very little after food and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which surprise has tested you lately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The washing machine failed in September, and we paid the repairer just before the school bus wages restarted. I put the rest of that week on a list and bought only what we needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the AI quiz help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me remember which warning belongs to the brake system and which belongs to cooling. I still open the manual before touching a machine, because a wrong answer underground is costly.

The mine should use saved time to improve **safety checks**.

feel: **Anxious** about existing income gaps and almost no reserve.

fieldNote: Her **term-time household income** and thin savings keep mortgage pressure alive even when AI has little effect.
Daily **AI quizzes** serve her learning, but she checks fault information against a manual before acting underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say dispatch and records will change first, and underground crews must check the plans. Workers should see the new targets before software quietly raises them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical haul runs probably continue, but a computer could tighten turnaround times. If the mine needs fewer dispatchers, my friend on that desk could lose hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test a new route planner on one shift with the surveyor beside me. I'd bring measured turnaround times to our union safety meeting if targets rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because the mine might turn a useful plan into a faster quota, and our household cannot lose paid shifts. I'm willing to try the tool early, but I want ground measurements beside the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd note the travel time through the narrow crosscut and how long clearing a spill really takes. If the planner assumes an empty route, the numbers could pressure someone to hurry under a bad roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the desk concerns you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Mara handles dispatch at night, and she knows which crosscuts flood after rain. Her judgement could be treated as a spare cost even while the software still needs her observations.

feel: **Anxious** about tighter targets and a colleague's hours.
S1.quote: If the planner assumes an empty route, the numbers could pressure someone to hurry under a bad roof.
fieldNote: She sees **desk work** changing before the scooptram, yet fears that software will raise physical production targets.
Her **eagerness to test** a route tool is paired with measurements of narrow passages and concern for a dispatcher she knows.

steps.text: Test route planner with surveyor during one underground shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew 2028 AGI could remove planning jobs before our machines change. The 2031 robots could run scooptrams, so workers need a paid route elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 in 2028, I may still be driving while dispatch becomes software. At 48 in 2031, I expect a smaller crew and my lower-paid seat could be cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enroll now in a water systems certificate offered evenings at the local college. I'd apply for nearby waterworks operator posts during the first robot year if scooptram shifts fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the timing, because the children will still be at home when the robots arrive and we have almost no buffer. A class gives me some control, though I cannot know whether the utility will hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you pay for that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union education fund for the first term and take one class at a time. My partner's bus contract cannot carry the mortgage if I stop mine work to study full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why water systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like tracing a pump fault, and the local treatment plant is a short ride from home. Robots might reach that work too, so I won't tell my children I've found a guaranteed safe job.

say: I'd tell the crew **2028 AGI** could remove planning jobs before our machines change.
The **2031 robots** could run scooptrams, so workers need a paid route elsewhere.
think: At 45 in **2028**, I may still be driving while dispatch becomes software.
At 48 in **2031**, I expect a smaller crew and my lower-paid seat could be cut.
do: Enroll now in a **water systems certificate** offered evenings at the local college.
Apply for nearby **waterworks operator** posts during the first robot year if scooptram shifts fall.
feel: **Anxious** about possible 2031 cuts, with a course to start.
S2.quote: My partner's bus contract cannot carry the mortgage if I stop mine work to study full-time.
fieldNote: She expects **2031 scooptram cuts** but uses the remaining years to begin a specific local qualification.
Her **thin cushion** rules out full-time study, and she admits that water operations may also change with robots.

steps.text: Enroll in one evening water systems class using union education funding
Apply for nearby waterworks operator posts if 2031 scooptram shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine to share a 2034 machine schedule now, not at the last crew meeting. Five years before AGI could fund joint training while operators still earn wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, AI could take over records and planning, but I'll likely still drive. At 51 in 2034, the children will be older and the mortgage may be smaller, yet I still need earnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first water systems module next autumn while keeping my mine shifts. I'd save the next two holiday-shift premiums toward one month of household expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still anxious about our current bank balance, though the longer warning lets me spread out the training. I could try the qualification without asking the children to move or giving up the mine wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the children see the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd see my course books on the kitchen table after dinner. I'd tell them I am learning because the machine job might change, not because someone has already taken it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine offers you a new robot job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd listen if it pays enough and comes with real instruction. I wouldn't count a control-room title as protection forever, because AGI could do that thinking work too.

think: At 48 in **2031**, AI could take over records and planning, but I'll likely still drive.

do: Take the first **water systems module** next autumn while keeping my mine shifts.

feel: **Anxious** about present savings despite more preparation time.
S3.quote: I wouldn't count a control-room title as protection forever, because AGI could do that thinking work too.
fieldNote: A **2034 robot arrival** gives her room to combine paid shifts, one course module and modest reserve building.
She does not treat a **control-room move** as permanently secure once AGI handles nearly all thinking work.

steps.text: Take first water systems module next autumn while working mine shifts
Save two holiday-shift premiums toward one month of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a 2039 robot date gives workers time to earn a second qualification. The mine should publish annual fleet numbers so families can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, AI may manage records while I can still drive the scooptram. At 56 in 2039, I cannot assume retirement or a robot-proof waterworks job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the scooptram wage while completing one water systems module next year. I'd check local utility vacancies every spring and ask what qualifications actually count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about bills now, but less frightened by a robot date thirteen years away. The children will be grown by then, and I could build a second skill while we still have mine income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave as soon as the certificate is done?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a paid offer that covers the mortgage. I can be curious about another job without turning our emergency money into a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What information would you trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dated mine fleet plan and the utility's written entry requirements. If either changes, I can change the order of the modules instead of paying for the wrong ones.

say: I'd say a **2039 robot date** gives workers time to earn a second qualification.
The mine should publish **annual fleet numbers** so families can plan.
think: At 53 in **2036**, AI may manage records while I can still drive the scooptram.
At 56 in **2039**, I cannot assume retirement or a robot-proof waterworks job.
do: Keep the **scooptram wage** while completing one water systems module next year.
Check local **utility vacancies** every spring and ask what qualifications actually count.
feel: **Anxious** about today's bills, with room for gradual training.
S4.quote: I can be curious about another job without turning our emergency money into a gamble.
fieldNote: Her **current financial strain** remains even when robot replacement is far into the future.
She balances **early learning** with strict protection of the mine wage and wants written job requirements before paying for modules.

steps.text: Take one water systems module next year while earning scooptram wages
Check utility vacancies and written qualification requirements each spring

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could reach the underground machines in 2031 while both children still need us and we have little saved. A funded evening course, written fleet dates, and a paid local opening would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to the people who keep the mine running during the transition. If training is only for office staff, the scooptram drivers will hear about their future when a robot arrives at the gate.

headlineQuote: If training is only for office staff, the scooptram drivers will hear about their future when a robot arrives at the gate.
portrait: Esther is a **43-year-old** experienced scooptram operator with a vocational certificate and lower mine pay.
A partner on **term-time bus wages**, two school-age children, a mortgage and thin savings make lost shifts costly.
She uses **AI daily** for equipment quizzes but verifies answers and tests new route tools against underground conditions.
She starts **water systems training** early while seeking written fleet plans and keeping the mine wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because 2031 robots could cut underground shifts before the family builds a reserve.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded evening course**, dated fleet plan and paid local opening would make a transition possible without missing mortgage payments.
